newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia's 1996 coal, crude oil output below target.
newsitem.headline: Serbia's 1996 coal, crude oil output below target.

text.p: Serbia produced around 37.098 million tonnes of coal in 1996, or 6.7 percent less than in the previous year, the Serbian Chamber of Commerce Energy Committee said in its latest report.

"The main reason output was below plan was lack of funds which prevented timely and necessary overhauls of mining mechanisation, transport and other equipment, coupled with growing claims," said Energy Committee secretary Radoje Zecevic.
Coal output last year fell 4.4 percent short of the target.
Zecevic said a slowdown in mining preparatory works could hinder output plans for 1997.
But coal output picked up in the first two months of the year to 7.221 million tonnes, or 6.3 percent more than in the same period last year and 10.2 percent above plan.
Crude oil output from local sources last year stood at 1.023 million tonnes, or three percent less than in 1995, the committee's report said.
An additional 241,491 tonnes of crude came from Angola, or eight percent more than in 1995.
January-February 1997 crude oil output from local sources stood at 158,325 tonnes, or 1.8 percent less than planned, and from Angola 42,800 tonnes, or 1.4 percent below target.
The report did not mention crude imports from China under a barter arrangement in exchange for Yugoslav products.
The drop in oil and natural gas production was attributed to exhausted deposits and insufficient investment in research and opening of new exploitation sites.
Outstanding claims were burdening oil producers as well, with Naftna Industrija Srbije (NIS) saying its claims had grown to 2.8 billion dinars.
"All winter we provided Elektroprivreda Srbije with gas and heating oil, and now they cannot pay us," NIS official Tosa Pavlovic said, referring to similar problems faced by Serbia's power company.
Industry sources appealed on the state to help resolve the problem of growing internal debts in the Yugoslav economy.
"The oil and power industry's claims from consumers have grown to nearly five billion dinars ($900 million), or nearly half of Serbia's budget," Zecevic said.
